steps.label: Do Now: Strings (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Strings (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy do programs often change text to capitals before comparing it?Show the answer

Then "Hi", "HI" and "hi" all count as the same word.

Recap of 2.5 String Manipulation. What does this program output?

DECLARE Word : STRING
Word ← "Upstander"
OUTPUT UCASE(Word)
OUTPUT LENGTH(Word)
Total: 2 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: UCASE and LENGTH

steps.text: UCASE changes every lower case letter to a capital. "Kind" becomes "KIND".
steps.visual: K i n d → K I N D

steps.text: Letters that are already capitals stay the same.
LENGTH counts the characters, one at a time: K, i, n, d.
So this program outputs KIND, then 4.
Now do the same for the question: capitals first, then count every character.

steps.label: Do Now: Following Pseudocode (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Following Pseudocode (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy do we trace a loop one value at a time?Show the answer

Then we can see exactly when Count changes, and why.

Recap of 3.1 Following and Correcting Pseudocode. What does this program output?

DECLARE Words : ARRAY[1:4] OF STRING
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
DECLARE i : INTEGER
Words[1] ← "hello"
Words[2] ← "ok"
Words[3] ← "thanks"
Words[4] ← "brilliant"
Count ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 4
    IF LENGTH(Words[i]) > 4 THEN
        Count ← Count + 1
    ENDIF
NEXT i
OUTPUT Count
Total: 1 mark

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: a loop over an array

steps.text: A similar question. The array holds "hi", "great", "no". Count goes up when a word has more than 2 characters.
"hi" has 2 characters. 2 is not more than 2, so Count stays 0.
"great" has 5 characters. 5 is more than 2, so Count becomes 1.
"no" has 2 characters, so Count stays 1. The loop ends and the program outputs 1.
Now do the same for the question: one word at a time, count the characters, compare with 4.

steps.label: Can Code Stop Cyberbullying?
steps.content:
Anti-Bullying Week

Can Code Stop Cyberbullying?

Year 9

Today: test a filter, see how fast a post spreads, and learn what an upstander does.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy might a school want a computer to check messages?Show the answer

There are too many messages for people to read them all.

steps.label: Mission 1: The Filter
steps.content:
Mission 1: The Filter

Think → Pair → ShareBefore you play: what kind of unkind message might a word filter miss?Show the answer

Take a few guesses, then test them in the game.

Niran wrote a filter for the class chat. Collect messages from people around the school and test it on your phone. Press Full screen for the best view.

steps.label: Explain It: Can a Filter Stop It?
steps.content:
Explain It: Can a Filter Stop It?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy do people have to test a program with real data?Show the answer

Real data has cases the programmer never thought of.

Explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked.

items.context: In the game, Niran's filter flagged any message with LOSER, UGLY, STUPID or WEIRDO inside it. It flagged harmless messages ("losers' bracket", "stupid slow laptop") and missed unkind ones ("l0s3r", sarcasm, "everyone except Sam"). In your own words, explain why a keyword filter cannot catch all cyberbullying.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain why a keyword filter cannot catch all cyberbullying.
scheme: It only checks for blocked words / letters, not what the message means
Unkind messages with no blocked word get through (sarcasm, leaving someone out, changed spellings)
Harmless messages that contain a blocked word get flagged (false alarms)
items.guidance: Any two points, one mark each, in the student's own words. An example counts as the point it shows. "It is not clever enough" alone earns nothing.
items.modelAnswer: It only looks for blocked words, not meaning. So "everyone except Sam" gets through, and "losers' bracket" gets flagged.

steps.label: Mission 2: One Screenshot
steps.content:
Mission 2: One Screenshot

Think → Pair → ShareBefore you play: if everyone forwards a post to 2 new people, how fast does it grow?Show the answer

Say a guess, then check it in the game.

Krit posted a screenshot of Sam. Find out how far one post can travel. Press Full screen for the best view.

steps.label: Explain It: Why Deleting Is Not Enough
steps.content:
Explain It: Why Deleting Is Not Enough

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does doubling grow so fast?Show the answer

Each step adds more new people than all the steps before it put together.

Explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked.

items.context: In the game, every person who got the screenshot forwarded it to 2 new people: 1, 3, 7, 15 people, and 255 after 8 steps. Then Krit deleted his post. In your own words, explain why deleting a post does not stop it spreading.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain why deleting a post does not stop it spreading.
scheme: Copies have already been forwarded / saved on other people's phones
Each person can forward it again, so it keeps spreading (it doubles each step)
items.guidance: One mark for each point, in the student's own words. "It is on the internet forever" alone earns 1 mark only if it says copies exist elsewhere.
items.modelAnswer: Other people already have copies on their phones, and each of them can forward it again.

steps.label: Mission 3: Be an Upstander
steps.content:
Mission 3: Be an Upstander

Think → Pair → ShareBefore you play: what is the difference between a bystander and an upstander?Show the answer

A bystander sees it and does nothing. An upstander does something to help.

The class chat is piling on Sam. Do the right things, in the right order. Press Full screen for the best view.

steps.label: Explain It: Evidence First
steps.content:
Explain It: Evidence First

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is replying in the chat a bad idea, even to defend someone?Show the answer

It can start an argument and give the people being unkind more attention.

Explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked.

items.context: In the game, the right order in the chat was: do not reply, save the evidence (a private screenshot), report it, then block, and tell a trusted adult. Blocking before saving lost the messages. In your own words, explain why you should save the evidence before you block someone.
items.prompt: In your own words, explain why you should save the evidence before you block someone.
scheme: Blocking can hide / remove the messages
An adult needs the evidence to see what happened and act on it
items.guidance: One mark for each point, in the student's own words. Saving evidence means keeping it privately for an adult; an answer about sharing or posting the screenshot earns nothing.
items.modelAnswer: Blocking can hide the messages. An adult needs to see them to help.

steps.label: Plenary: Upstander Drill
steps.content:
Plenary: Upstander Drill

Think → Pair → ShareWhy practise with new messages every time?Show the answer

Then you know how the filter works, not just the game's messages.

Filters, false alarms and misses, how far posts spread, and what an upstander does. Your progress is saved.

steps.label: Where to Get Help
steps.content:
Where to Get Help

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is telling an adult not "snitching"?Show the answer

It is how bullying actually stops, and it protects the person being targeted.

If anything online is worrying you, or someone you know:

  • Talk to your form tutor, any teacher you trust, or the school counsellor.
  • Save the messages, report and block. Do not reply.
  • You will not get in trouble for telling.
